tracks.title: Proof that travels with the file
tracks.text: Lesson one point six — sharing… a deep dive under the workbook lesson. The parent lesson ended on a one-liner. You type w b x sign, shop dot html… and the answer comes back: signed — provenance travels with the file. [curious] This episode is the how. How does proof ride inside a file? What exactly gets proven… to whom… with what key? And one promise to hold me to, all the way through: no account on either end. Not for the sender. Not for the recipient.

tracks.title: From: you, unverified
tracks.text: First — the problem. From: you… unverified. The parent lesson convinced you of something genuinely unusual: you can email someone your app. And the moment you believe that, two fears arrive — one on each side of the handoff. The sender's fear… once the file leaves, anyone can alter it, and the altered thing still carries your name. The recipient's mirror image… this arrived as an HTML attachment from the internet. Why would anyone trust an HTML attachment's claim about who made it? [sighs] Every answer software has built so far authenticates something other than the file. HTTPS authenticates the pipe — forward the download, and the proof evaporates. App stores authenticate a distributor — for the price of an account, a review queue, and a platform. Code signing authenticates through certificate chains that lead back to an authority somebody paid. Channel trust… distributor trust. All of it needs infrastructure standing by at verification time. But a file forwarded over email has no channel left, and no distributor at all. If the proof does not ride in the bytes… there is no proof.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. Sharing… noun. Handing over a workbook with the maker's cryptographic identity riding in the file. Signed on the way out… verifiable by anyone… no account on either end. And it happens on two rails, worth keeping distinct from the start. The source rail — the unpacked repo, pushed as plain git, to any host. And the artifact rail — the packed, signed workbook, handed to any surface. History rides the source. Proof rides the artifact. We take the proof apart first… because nothing else in software does it quite this way.

tracks.title: One key, every claim
tracks.text: One key, every claim. Everything starts smaller than you might expect. Every tenant has exactly one Ed25519 keypair — generated by the runtime's own crypto, stored in the tenant's keystore… and the private half never enters version control, because the same module that guards every exit writes a gitignore over the whole keystore automatically. The public half becomes a name — and this is the load-bearing move of the entire lesson. Take the thirty-two byte public key… prefix it with a two-byte tag that says, this is Ed25519… encode the result in base fifty-eight… and put the letter z on the front. What you get reads: did, colon, key, colon, z six M k… and then a long string of characters. That is a real W three C did key — the same form Radicle uses, interoperable rather than bespoke — and here is the part to sit with. [excited] That long string is not a username pointing at a key stored somewhere. It IS the public key. The name and the key are the same bytes. They never separated… so no registry has to connect them. Now picture that one key at the center, fanning out to four claims. One: artifact manifests — the signed workbook files, this episode's subject. Two: the agent ledger head — the same key signing the record of what the agents did… that one has its own lesson. Three: the did web document — the same key, published at a domain… coming later in this episode. And four: toolkit provenance — third-party installs, covered in the trust lesson. One identity… every proof in the ecosystem leans on it. And one more branch, in a single sentence: the same identity can also receive secrets — the key converts to an encryption key by a standard mapping, so a sealed bundle can be locked to a recipient's DID with no second key published. The mechanics of that rung live in the escrow lesson… not here.

tracks.title: What happens at the handoff
tracks.text: What happens at the handoff. Signing embeds a manifest — one script block, tucked in just before the closing body tag of the HTML. Crack a signed file open and you find a small JSON object. Let me read it to you, field by field. Version… v one. Issuer did… the maker's did key — and because the DID is the public key, this field doubles as the verification key. Claim generator… the software that signed — the runtime, or the local CLI… same manifest either way. Issued at… the timestamp. Asset sha two fifty-six… the hash of the HTML with this block removed — and that removal is how a file can contain its own hash without a paradox. Assertions… what is being claimed — published, by this actor. And signature… Ed25519, over the manifest in canonical form — keys sorted, compact, U T F eight… one byte contract, implemented identically in Elixir, Rust, and JavaScript. The byte-level details belong to the signatures lesson… this episode stays at the handshake. So picture the handoff as three actors. The sender runs w b x sign… the manifest block lands in the file. The file travels — mail, chat, a USB stick… the channel proves nothing, and does not need to. It arrives at the recipient as bytes… and the recipient runs exactly two checks. Check one: the Ed25519 signature, under the key the DID itself encodes. Check two: the hash of the file, minus the manifest, equals the hash the manifest recorded. Either one fails… the file is invalid. Both pass… valid, with the issuer's DID and the claims. And notice who was never contacted — the sender. Two small details worth keeping. Signing is idempotent — re-signing strips any prior manifest first, so a file never accumulates stale claims. And both command lanes — the engine CLI and the local one — are byte compatible… either can verify the other's output.

tracks.title: Single authentication
tracks.text: Now a depth rung — single authentication… why there is no certificate chain. The manifest's shape is borrowed from C two P A — the content provenance standard the camera industry uses. But full C two P A authenticates identity through X five oh nine. Your key is vouched for by a certificate… the certificate by an authority… the authority by a trust list. This design deliberately superseded that path — the spike's own words: we adopt the scheme… drop the machinery. [chuckles] The whole comparison comes down to two cells. Under X five oh nine, verify means: walk the chain, check each signature along it, then match the subject to the claimed identity. Under did key, verify means: decode the DID… one signature check… done. Because the DID is the key, the two questions — is the signature valid, and does the key belong to the claimed identity — collapse into one operation. There is no gap for a second check to cover. That is what single authentication means. And the honest cell on the other side: revocation. X five oh nine could say, stop trusting this key. A did key has no way to say that… we come back to it in the limits.

tracks.title: Verify with nothing installed
tracks.text: Verify with nothing installed — the episode's load-bearing promise, so let's keep it literal. Here is the round trip, spoken. You run w b x sign on shop dot html… it answers: signed, as your did key. You run w b x verify… and back comes a verdict object: valid, true. Signature, true. Asset integrity, true. Issuer — your DID. Now the tamper demo. Someone edits one character of the page… and runs verify again. Valid, false. Signature… still true. Asset integrity… false. [curious] Read that split carefully, because it is the diagnostic. Signature true, integrity false means: the manifest is genuinely hers… and the bytes were touched after she signed. If the tamperer instead re-signs the altered file with their own key — both checks go green… but the issuer flips to THEIR DID. The attacker can have your name, or a valid signature. Never both. And the verifier itself… the entire consumer side is one file, verify dot m j s. About seventy-seven lines. Zero dependencies — browser crypto and base sixty-four decoding, nothing else. It runs in a modern browser or Node twenty and up… returns a plain verdict… never throws. One line at a terminal — no install, no account, no runtime — and the verdict prints. [excited] And those seventy-seven lines are not a toy edition of something bigger. They replaced a four hundred eighty-three line verifier from the archive — the claim-chain walker, the envelope decoding, the per-assertion canonicalization, all dropped… because every one of them existed to bridge a key-to-identity gap that a self-certifying DID does not have.

tracks.title: Signed on every way out
tracks.text: Signed on every way out. Here is what keeps signing from becoming one more step humans forget… you mostly never run w b x sign at all. The engine signs as part of leaving. Three doors, all passing through the same seam. First: ship. Packing a bundle signs the workbook HTML as part of the pack — the bundle's label records signed, true… and a shipped bundle's provenance is checkable on arrival. Second: checkin. Returning a borrowed workbook to the library re-signs it, with an updated assertion — so the borrow and return is on the record. Third: the install gate. A library can demand a valid signature… and then installing a third-party member refuses on an invalid manifest. [chuckles] The consequence reads small, and is not. By the time a workbook is anywhere another person could receive it… the question, did anyone remember to sign this — has no unsigned answer. Provenance is a property of leaving… not a ceremony you remember.

tracks.title: The two rails
tracks.text: The two rails. A workbook leaves home in two forms, and they answer different questions. Picture the repo at the top — your work, with its history — and two lanes flowing out of it. Down the first lane, the source rail: plain git, pushed anywhere. One command mirrors the repo to any remote… pass a forge flag, and GitHub, GitLab, or Gitea is provisioned automatically through that host's own tooling. No proprietary sync… no blessed forge. Down the second lane, the artifact rail: the packed, signed workbook — handed to a static page, your own server, or an A T proto feed, where the publish toolkit binds a Bluesky account and runs a provenance-verified feed. The split to remember: history rides the source… proof rides the artifact. A git host vouches for nothing — and does not need to, because the artifact carries its own vouching. And underneath both rails, one precondition this ecosystem treats as non-negotiable: sharing exposes the work… never the session that produced it. The manifest travels. The agent's session ledger and telemetry stay home. Proof of origin and exposure of process are different things… and only the first one ships.

tracks.title: Share by identity, not bytes
tracks.text: Now the upper rung — share by identity, not bytes. Everything so far handed over bytes. This rung hands over a name. A workspace member can be a DID reference — a property on a headline — and checkout resolves it to bytes when needed. For that to work, a DID has to be findable… and here the design is honest about its own primitive. A bare did key has no inherent location. The resolver says so in its own error message — locating one needs a registry anchor, which is an extension… not a shipped promise. What IS shipped is the HTTPS rail — did web. The same key — not a second identity — republished as a document at a well-known path on your domain. Fetch it, and you hear three things. The verification key… lifted byte for byte from the did key — the same z six M k string. An also-known-as field… cross-linking the did key, so a signature verifies under either DID. And a service entry called WorkbookHost… pointing at where the workbooks live. [curious] Which turns the identity into an address. Resolution is a four-step story. A resolver fetches the did document over HTTPS… reads the key and the cross-link… follows the service endpoint to the workbook bytes… and verifies the manifest — valid under either DID. One more federation rail exists, with its caveat attached: Radicle, the peer-to-peer network. The engine can publish a repo there and hand back a rad ID… but Radicle's keys are per device — an upstream limitation, so the tenant key is not the delegate identity yet — and a cross-machine clone needs at least two nodes, or a seed peer. Real… reachable… not yet the smooth rail did web is.

tracks.title: What a signature doesn't promise
tracks.text: What a signature does not promise — the honesty section. Five edges, each one load-bearing. First… signed is not safe. A signature proves origin and integrity — who, and untouched since. Never goodness. A signed workbook can still be malicious — the maker just cannot deny making it. The layer that bounds the damage is the sandbox… two layers, on purpose. Provenance tells you who to blame. Isolation limits what there is to blame them for. Second… signed is not private. The manifest authenticates the bytes — it does nothing to hide them. Hiding is the privacy strip and sealed sections, each with its own lesson. Third… no revocation. The certificate machinery this design dropped included the one thing it did well — a way to say, stop trusting this key. A did key has no such channel. A signature, once out, verifies forever under that DID. Fourth… lose the seed, lose the identity. [exhales] The flip side of self-certifying: no authority can reissue you. Concretely — a redeploy wipes the container filesystem, and the tenant's keypair is restored from one secret… W B SIGNING KEY, holding the seed. Without it, the redeploy mints a NEW DID… and every prior signature stops being yours. That one secret is the identity's continuity. Treat it like the key it literally is. And fifth… carriers keep their own identities. Publishing to A T proto means a second DID — Bluesky's, on a different curve entirely — and the two do not unify. The answer: sign with the did key BEFORE the carrier… the embedded manifest binds the two. Bound… not merged… is the honest verb.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire — questions people actually ask. Do I need a Workbooks account to verify? No. That is the point of the whole design… the DID is the key, so verification needs the file and nothing else. What if I lose my key? Then that identity is over — no recovery, no reissue, because there is no authority to do the reissuing. A new key is a new DID… your old signatures still verify under the old one — you just cannot add to them. Can I have the same identity on two machines? Yes — the identity is thirty-two bytes of seed, and the publish toolkit's identity verbs export and import it… the private half only when you ask for it explicitly. Is this C two P A? The scheme… not the machinery. The manifest speaks its vocabulary — minus the certificate chain, plus a self-certifying DID. Does signing make my workbook tamper-proof? [chuckles] Tamper-evident… not tamper-proof. Anyone can edit the bytes, or strip the manifest entirely. What they cannot do is keep a valid manifest under YOUR DID afterward. And last — can someone re-sign my work and claim it? They can publish your bytes under their own DID — a signature proves who signed, not who authored first. What they can never produce is a valid manifest under your DID… and what you always have is your earlier signature, with its earlier timestamp.

tracks.title: Back up to the parent
tracks.text: So that is sharing. A key that became a name… a name that is the key… and a file that carries its own proof — signed on every way out, checkable by anyone, with no account on either side of the handoff. [chuckles] And honestly bounded: tamper-evident, not tamper-proof… provenance, not safety… and one secret standing between your identity and a fresh start you did not ask for. The way back up is short. This was a deep dive under lesson one — what is a workbook… the page where provenance travels with the file was a single line of terminal output. And when you want the byte-level mechanics underneath this episode — the canonical JSON, the exact signing dance — the signatures lesson picks up precisely where this one stops.
